# Phase 4 — Structure, prose, and voice (editor's own pass on v2, written before the Phase 1, 2, and 5 reports were read)

Near-final stage: line-level craft included. Line numbers refer to `drafts/v2.md`. Round-1 figures are from `correspondence/v1-review/04-craft-notes.md` for comparison.

## Measurements

| Measure | v1 | v2 | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| Body words | 11,891 | 16,000 | Corpus ceiling 12,250 (*Visibility*); manifest tolerance 12,000. Over by ~4,000 |
| Words before §X | ~7,400 (62%) | 9,978 (62%) | Unchanged share; the corpus long form spends 30–50% before the contemporary payoff |
| §XI–§XIV (the essay's own apparatus) | 2,049 (17%) | 3,692 (23%) | Improved; the constructive half is no longer starved |
| Longest section | §I 1,276 | §III 2,367 | §III doubled; it is now the longest section by 1,000 words |
| Shortest numbered section | §XIII 300 | §XV 563 | §XIII now 647 and runs the test on a live case |
| One-sentence paragraphs | 18 of 137 (13%) | 15 of 135 (11%) | In range |
| Sentences ≥40 words | 78 of 488 (16%) | 120 of 665 (18%) | Worse; 34 sentences run 60+ words. Corpus target ≤10% |
| "This essay / the essay" | 23 | 41 | Up 78%; one per 390 words |
| Section cross-references | 27 | 18 | Forward pointers cut as asked |
| References to the predecessor essays ("the previous essay in this series," etc.) | 9 | 10 | l.40, l.56, l.148, l.154, l.180, l.238, l.248, l.274, l.298, l.304 |
| Negation→short-correction cadence ("not X. It is Y.") | ~25 | ~13 | Halved as asked; the survivors carry distinctions |
| Coined or marked terms | 9 | 4 italicized (*externalized forum internum*, *cognitive legibility*, *epistemic exit*, *behavioral legibility* [inherited]) + 6 named without italics (cognitive record, probability shaping, permissioned cognition, the complex, constitutional half-life, minimum necessary legibility, archival reachability) | Marked coinages reduced as asked; the named-things count is unchanged |

## Structure (developmental)

**The opening still earns the reader's five minutes, and the corrected chronology costs nothing.** l.10 now reads as OpenAI's own timeline (late May; July; disclosed July 21; accounted for Aug. 26), the deliberate switch-off is in, Klonick's deflationary reading is conceded in a clause, and the SaferAI corroboration at l.14 takes the exit half off Hugging Face's word alone. l.16 is the right moral now ("It is about what dependence costs when the guardian is not answerable, and what it is worth to have somewhere else to go"), and "The sovereign version of that problem … is the essay's" hands the state-shaped claim to §V where it is earned. The conceptual turn ("That question is not wrong. It is second.") lands at l.18, ~900 words in: the *Visibility* delay, and it works. The new tense paragraph (l.20) is a scope paragraph in the corpus's third-person form and it pays off (the record at l.84; the "one month of 2026" at l.210). One fault: l.20 is 200 words and the sentence beginning "The composed architecture the later sections describe" runs 70 words with two embedded glosses ("the layer at which a system is administered rather than used"; "anticipatory rather than accusatory"); the gloss of "control plane" is right to have and wrong to have here, where the reader has not met the term.

**Proportion: the history is exactly as front-loaded as before, for a different reason.** v1's 62 percent came from §I; v2's comes from §III, which grew from ~1,100 to 2,367 words while §I shrank by 200 and the constructive sections grew by 1,600. §III now does four jobs in sequence: the field (l.66–78, ~1,050 words: Bublitz, Richards, Shaheed, Ienca & Andorno, Farahany, Alegre, Boire/Sententia, the coinage, Blitz, Bublitz again, Ligthart, De Cock), the third-party doctrine (l.80, ~250), the record (l.82–84, ~500), and chilling (l.86–90, ~320). The author asks which the essay can afford to lose. My reading, before the discourse report: the survey sentence-run at l.68 (a 235-word paragraph that names five scholars in the register of a literature review) is the only movement that does no work later in the essay; Blitz, Bublitz, Ligthart, and De Cock at l.74–76 *are* the argument (the extension claimed, the objection answered, the absoluteness relocated, the rival coinage distinguished) and should stay at length; l.80 does work nothing else does (access versus retention, which §XIII depends on); l.84 is the essay's strongest evidence. So: l.68 to two sentences (Ienca & Andorno's four rights and Milton line; Alegre's inversion), with Farahany, Sententia and Boire, and the Rapporteur's "relayed submission" carried in the reference notes (−250); l.84 to its four strongest items (the preservation order and the twenty million; the Maine warrant; the referral policy; *Heppner*), with *Kim*, the tripled requests, and Altman moved to a note (−150). That takes §III to ~1,950 and keeps all four jobs.

- **§I (1,062 words)** is shorter and better: Bayle and Locke share a paragraph, Milton has one quotation, Kant and Mill keep their length, and the "delegation surrenders judgment where collaboration exercises it" inference (l.36) is now made rather than asserted. It can still lose ~250: the Bayle "difficulty is famous" sentence and Forst's reply (l.28) are a scholarly aside the essay never uses; Locke's exclusions (another prince; atheists) are the corpus's "Mufti" anecdote and can be a clause.
- **§IV and §XV no longer duplicate.** §XV (l.294–298) is now the place the thinkers are used on the layers ("At the first and fifth layers … Berlin's presumption is enough. At the third layer … Pettit's question is the live one. At the fourth layer … Spinoza's line"), which is what the round-1 letter asked for and it is the right shape. But l.296 is one 210-word paragraph assigning seven thinkers, and the assignment is asserted, not argued: why Spinoza at layer 4 rather than Kant (the guardian who is not answerable is the local model's trainer as much as the hosted provider's)? Rushed crux; two paragraphs, not one.
- **§V's exit paragraph (l.122) is the round's largest single addition and its most crowded paragraph:** 470 words carrying eight distinct moves (exit is plural or nothing; the shaping is in the weights; a local copy answers the record; *Heppner*; Palermos; Beijing as sovereignty not liberty; exit to a weaker model; the state's positive duties, OpenAI's republican reply, Montana). It reads as a ledger being cleared. Three paragraphs: (i) record versus shaping and what local inference actually buys; (ii) plurality among trainers and Beijing; (iii) the state as guarantor, the republican reply answered by layer, Montana as the statute. The "cellar press" figure returns here for the third time (l.120, l.122 twice); the corpus runs an analogy for two to five sentences and drops it.
- **§VI (912)** is the corpus's best-attested history and the round-1 cuts (Lessig's opening sequence; two Clipper details) cost nothing. The Kill Switch Act now sits at l.144 as the live instance of "remotely revocable capability," which is exactly where it belongs; Lu's metrics/content line named as "minimum necessary legibility" is a clean handoff to §XII.
- **§X (1,298)** now carries the September positions (l.208) and the June practice (l.210) in two 190-word paragraphs of dense record. The record register is the lawyer's, per the corpus, and it is fine here; what is not fine is l.208's roll-call sentence (OpenAI … "demands more than voluntary commitments" … "mandatory, capability-based" … "America needs both" … signed the July letter … which Anthropic did not sign), 74 words with four quotations and two parties, followed immediately by Zuckerberg. Split at the signatory clause.
- **§XI (863)** is improved by the Sastry citation with its one-sentence statement of what the eight questions add (l.228), and by the layer-5 concession (l.234). The concession paragraph is the section's crux and its longest paragraph (200 words); the two-object distinction ("A log of what a system did at an interface is a different object from a log of what a person asked it") deserves its own short paragraph, not a clause after "The concession sharpens the rule rather than defeating it."
- **§XII (1,396).** The eight questions as short paragraphs are the corpus's enumeration form (*Visibility*'s nine thresholds) and they read well; "A law can expire faster than the architecture constructed to enforce it" (l.254) is the section's aphorism. The problem is l.260: 420 words, one paragraph, carrying the essay's crux (the layer-2 run: passes 1, 2, 3, 5; strains 4 and 7; "fails both outright" with a single tester; the four conditions; "the bargain of 1557") *and* the Kill Switch Act run *and* the "use pattern" question. The paragraph the essay exists to write is the middle third of a paragraph. Three paragraphs: the layer-2 run; the verdict and its conditions; the bill. And the sentence "The proposal that passes most cleanly is, unexpectedly, the one that sounds most like a kill switch" is the best against-interest line in the section and is currently buried.
- **§XIII (647)** now runs the test on the verified tier (l.276) and counts ("Two of the four conditions are present … That is what the diagnosis is for: not to announce that the structure exists, but to count"). That last sentence is the right ending for the section. l.272's "Legibility achieved privately is a present harm of the kind the fourth section named … and a latent harm of the sovereign kind" answers the second reader's round-1 objection in one sentence.
- **§XIV (786)** is labeled as a construction ("What follows is a construction, and that should be said plainly") in the corpus's own form, and l.286 names the three built components. l.286 is 230 words in one paragraph with two citations bundles ([81][80]; [75][69][1][54]); the four-marker bundle at "the remote shutdown came in a bill.[75][69][1][54]" is the essay's only citation pile-up and reads as a defense.
- **The ending.** The three endings are gone: l.306 folds the *Constitution of Reason* motif into a clause ("because no model, no company, no state, and no safety institution is identical with reason") and l.308 is three sentences, the last two the right last two. l.304's "the previous essay in this series described how far the inference now reaches" is the tenth predecessor reference and the coda is the wrong place for it.

**Title and subtitle.** Unchanged; the author kept the writer's title under autonomy and recorded the alternative. "The Governable Mind" / "…the Constitutional Limits of the Legible Mind" still puts "Mind" twice and two adjectives on one noun. Open question for the author, not a finding. Section titles are all declarative or noun phrases; "XV. No Sovereign Layer" now names what the section argues.

## Prose (line level) — patterns with exemplars

**1. The chained record sentence (new; the round's main prose cost).** The sections the specialist readers will read most closely are the ones where sentences now run longest: 18 percent at 40+ words, 34 at 60+, nearly all in the record and policy paragraphs added this round. The corpus's catalogue sentence is legitimate (a list wearing a sentence); these chain facts, quotations, dates, and citations.
- l.84 (78 words): "A magistrate judge in the *New York Times*'s copyright suit ordered OpenAI in May 2025 'to preserve and segregate all output log data that would otherwise be deleted,' so that for four months no consumer's deletion of a conversation took effect, and in January 2026 the district judge affirmed the production of twenty million de-identified conversations, reasoning that the privacy interest in conversations 'which users voluntarily disclosed to OpenAI' is weaker than the interest in a wiretapped call."
- l.206 (90 words): "OpenAI and Anthropic now relax their cyber safeguards for defenders who verify who they are, with a government identity document, through the same verification vendor; Anthropic's most capable current model is available 'to vetted cyberdefenders and life scientists through our trusted access programs,' and for now only to 'a set of US organizations'; OpenAI's verification, its own help pages say, 'does not support retries or appeals,' and in August researchers outside the United States and Europe found their access withdrawn with the notice that their identity 'could not be verified.'"
- l.122 (75 words): "Nothing a person asks it leaves the machine, which is why the ruling of February 2026 turned on the ground it did, that the exchanges were unprivileged because a third party held them on its own terms, a ground a model on the defendant's own hardware would not have supplied; and it is why a philosopher of the extended mind has argued that mental data should be made 'practically—not just legally—impossible for others to obtain.'"
Rewritten (l.84): "In May 2025 a magistrate judge in the *New York Times*'s copyright suit ordered OpenAI 'to preserve and segregate all output log data that would otherwise be deleted.' For four months no consumer's deletion of a conversation took effect. In January 2026 the district judge affirmed the production of twenty million de-identified conversations, reasoning that the privacy interest in conversations 'which users voluntarily disclosed to OpenAI' is weaker than the interest in a wiretapped call." Three sentences, the same facts, the quotation given room.

**2. The essay narrating its own moves (new; replaces the forward pointer).** The forward pointers were cut as asked, and "this essay / the essay" rose from 23 to 41. The corpus uses "this essay" for commitments in place of a first person; v2 uses it to stage-manage concessions and pivots, so that the reader is told the essay is conceding rather than shown the concession.
- l.76: "That reply commits the essay to a position."
- l.190: "The dissociation cuts both ways, and the essay accepts the cut."
- l.208: "It would be convenient to dismiss the safety argument as regulatory capture, and the essay declines the convenience."
- l.122: "The essay agrees, where the standards govern datacenters and interfaces to the world."
- l.100: "The essay uses both."
- l.262: "The essay's own preference, for the protection of local inference, must answer the first question as squarely as anyone."
- l.212: "That is the constitutional boundary this essay exists to locate."
Rewritten (l.190): "The dissociation cuts both ways: an intermediary that works in language cannot make a thought impossible, which is exactly why the claim here is about availability and not about determinism." The concession is made by making it. Cut roughly half of the 41; keep the ones that state a commitment ("this essay argues," "as this essay uses the term").

**3. The negation-correction cadence: fixed, and worth saying so.** Down from ~25 to ~13, and the survivors carry distinctions: "That question is not wrong. It is second." (l.18); "The genre is not wrong about the companies. It is wrong about the word." (l.108); "It is not, in the first instance, censorship. It is concentration." (l.126); "it is not about impossibility. It is about probability." (l.186); "does not need a new name. It is pluralism." (l.294). No quota was applied and none should be.

**4. "And it is the one" (new tic, small).** A relative flourish that appears at l.10 ("and it is the one the safety literature had been predicting"), l.12 ("and it is less often told"), l.176 ("and it is the one closest to this essay's subject"), l.260 ("and it is the one actually proposed"). Four is enough for a reader to hear it. Keep l.260's (it does work); cut the others to the plain clause.

**5. The quotation mosaic in the survey register.** l.68 is a 235-word paragraph built from six quoted fragments across five authors; l.204 (IASR) is four quotations in 160 words; l.208 is four in 74. In the record paragraphs the mosaic is the lawyer's register the corpus attests (*Visibility*) and earns its place; in l.68 it is a literature review in an essay, and the corpus's citation style is "name the author and the claim in the sentence" once, not fragments. Rewritten (l.68, the Farahany sentence): "Nita Farahany, whose book made cognitive liberty a current term, defines it as self-determination over one's own brain and mental experience; her subject is the brain read or altered directly, and where she reaches generative artificial intelligence it is as a manipulator of belief." Same content, no quotation, one clause fewer.

**6. Numerals and consistency (small).** "nineteen days" (l.210) against "eighteen days" (l.276, l.290): the author's response explains (eighteen to lifting, nineteen to restoration) and the text does not; a reader will call it an error. "17,600" (l.10) against "seventeen thousand" (l.234). "about twenty by press accounts" (l.210) is the right hedge and should be matched by the ref [76] count (the cited Tech Times piece says twelve days where the text says two weeks; Phase 1 will rule).

**7. Terms before they are earned: fixed.** "control plane" glossed at l.20 (though in the wrong sentence, above); "attested hardware (hardware that proves to a remote party what it is running)" at l.144; "approved signatures, cryptographic marks a machine can be made to check" at l.282. "Persona" the vendor is never named (l.206 says "the same verification vendor"), which is the right call given the ledger's round-1 finding that the consumer-tier claim was unsupported.

**8. Self-certification: fixed, one survivor by design.** "The honest caveat belongs beside the fact" (l.178) stays as the persona's attested construction; "should be said plainly" (l.280) is the corpus's own labeling form. "the essay declines the convenience" (l.208) is pattern 2 above.

## Voice

**There is one, and it is consistent**: the reported-political-analysis register of *The Politics of Visibility* (documented opening, a lawyer's evidentiary care, intellectual history run forward, a constructive apparatus, a falsification list), with zero first person and "this essay" as the agent. The register is right for the argument and the audience, and the new record paragraphs (l.84, l.210) are where the piece sounds most like *someone*: "A record its keeper calls uniquely private, a court calls voluntarily disclosed, and a prosecutor obtains by ordinary warrant is the object this section has been defining, and it exists" (l.84) is the best new sentence in the draft. Where it sounds like everyone: l.68 (the survey), l.296 (the roll-call), and the middle of l.260, where the crux is written in the same even tone as the runway around it.

**Earned versus unearned authority.** Earned: "unexpectedly" at l.260, which marks a result the essay did not want; "That is what the diagnosis is for … to count" (l.276); the falsification clause now carrying its first data (l.290). Claimed beyond what the text establishes: "The first documented instance is already on the record" (l.152), a superlative that Phase 1 is checking; "the same state supplies the essay's most detailed demonstration" (l.122) is fine; "Identity as a condition of capable hosted inference now exists in two forms" (l.276) asserts more than the two instances support (see Phase 3: one form was lifted after eighteen days and the other conditions an exception to a safeguard, not access to the model). The essay's authority in §XII–§XIV rests on counting honestly; l.276 and l.290 are where the count is most generous to the thesis.

**Persona note (not a finding).** The ten predecessor references are a deliberate departure from the essays' no-self-citation rule, recorded as open in the author's response (flag 2). The form used (relative reference in prose, title in the apparatus) is the corpus's one attested form. The count is the reader's concern only insofar as a cold reader is sent elsewhere; the three imports that carried weight are now stated in the essay's own sentences (chilling as the injury that leaves no defendant, l.86; behavioral legibility defined, l.148; "no finite mind is reason as such," l.40), so the cold reader is no longer sent away. Divergence is not a defect; the decision is the author's.
